Their Smart 50 Awards are provided to the top 50 Smart Cities projects from around the world each year and are presented at an awards gala at their annual conference.

Travel restrictions from COVID had kept us from attending in 2021 and 2022.

collaboration, engagement, use of our innovation lab, and the application of emerging technology.

That's top level recognition that makes me very proud of the work that
our staff are doing and the recognition we're receiving for it.
The project submission for Growing Together was a collaboration between the City's Planning and Technology, Innovation and Services divisions.
I'm joined today by Adam Clark and Courtney Zinn from Planning and Digital Kitchener Innovation Lab, respectively,
who have collaborated together to deliver on this project and prepared the project submission for the Smart 50 Awards.
Through the Growing Together project, the Digital Kitchener Innovation Lab and City Planning staff
have developed an accurate 3D printed model of key areas of the city and
generic representations of buildings of specific sizes and realistic styles.
Through hands-on workshops the community can engage with the 3D model to develop
scenarios for growth. Those scenarios are then translated into the digital model
and enabling a wealth of information and metrics to be generated including
density, housing, number of people, jobs, green space and more. Effectively
translating the community vision into a quantifiable impact. The project is also
exploring how emerging technologies can further complement this work. A prototype
has been created of an augmented reality application to blend the physical and
digital worlds. Through the app users can visualize the digital 3D models in the
context of the 3D printed model through a phone or tablet to create an
understanding of how new proposals may fit into an existing area. The project
continues to explore how technologies can support the city in tackling complex
and challenging issues like housing and urban growth and create opportunities
for community engagement and data informed outcomes. We'd now be honored to
present both the Smart 50 award and the top three award certificate to Mayor
on behalf of Council.

The first item on this evening's agenda is Strategic Plan 2019-2022 with the Compass Kitchener
report card and I'd like to welcome Judy Stevens-Walls and Troy Glover from our Compass Kitchener
Advisory Committee. Welcome Judy and welcome Troy. It's great to have you both back. Thank you very
much. Thank you. Good evening Mayor Vrbanovic and members of Council. It's a pleasure to be here
again this evening. As you all know Compass Kitchener is a committee of citizen volunteers
appointed by and reporting directly to City Council. The roles and responsibilities
assigned to our committee all focus on assisting with the development of the
City's strategic plan and then evaluating implementation of the strategic
plan and reporting back to Council on the results of that evaluation. Compass
Kitchener is currently comprised of 11 citizens, nine of whom were able to
participate in this recent evaluation process. The two who were not available
to do so have been marked with an asterisk. The committee is supported in

thank Angie Fritz-Walters and Linda Carabo for the amazing job they do in
supporting Compass Kitchener in the work that we do. In terms of the evaluation
approach we take the viewpoint of interested citizens and considered timing,
impact, accountability and budget in undertaking this evaluation? Answering
the following questions guided the evaluation. Timing, were the strategic
actions completed in the expected timeframe? Impact, how did the strategic
actions deliver on anticipated or desired impacts? How did progress on or
completion of strategic actions make a difference to the city or to citizens?
Accountability, were progress reports relevant, timely and publicly profiled?
How well was the public engaged?
And Budget, were the strategic actions completed on or within budget?
Of those four elements, the middle two, impact and accountability, are really the heart of the matter.
Compass Kitchener developed a specific citizen impact criteria for each strategic action
and consulted with Kitchener's corporate leadership team as it did so.
Our pre-circulated written report provides a lot more detailed information, but given the time available this evening, we can only touch on some key highlights.
Our first report card regarding the 2019-2022 strategic plan was presented to Council in December of 2021.
In it, we evaluated 12 completed projects and provided a number of recommendations.
And as you can see in the slide of those 12 that were evaluated, six exceeded our expectations and the other six met our expectations.
This year, Compass Kitchener has undertaken a review of five projects completed in 2022.
The Energy Efficient Reserve Fund, the Sustainable Urban Forest Strategy, the Waste Diversion Strategy, Huron Community Centre, and Communication of Service Levels.
Unfortunately, one completed project, the Customer Experience Review Program, was not included in either of our 2021 or 2022 report cards.
The program was completed in 2021 after we finished our 2021 evaluation process.
Its exclusion from the 2022 report card was an unintended oversight.
Rest assured, it will be reviewed during our next round of project evaluations.
Given time constraints, I will just touch on highlights of each assessment.
Performance on the Energy Efficiency Reserve Fund met expectations.
Compass Kitchener determined investments in energy savings projects are having a positive
financial impact.
Also, several projects came under budget and there is a healthy balance for future investment.
on the sustainable urban forest strategy exceeded expectations. Compass Kitchener determined the
strategy is comprehensive with its extensive public engagement in exemplary public education,
partnership, and communication. Moreover, it set an ambitious yet achievable tree canopy goal,
and it eliminated an existing backlog with the planting of over 2,600 trees.
Performance on the city's waste diversion strategy did not meet expectations.
While it established a welcome collaboration between the city and researchers at Wilfrid Laurier University,
pilot results suggest the decision to discontinue the strategy is a good one.
Compass Kitchener recommends that the city review and perhaps even renegotiate
responsibilities for waste diversion between the region and itself if
possible. Performance related to Huron Community Center exceeded expectations.
Compass Kitchener deemed it a very successful strategic collaboration
between partners. Its partnerships enabled more amenities to be included as
result of economies of scale. Huron Community Center offers lessons that
should be applied to future community center builds in the city. And finally,
performance related to setting and communicating service levels did not meet
expectations. Compass Kitchener determined the city needs to proactively make
service standards more public by sharing information on how service level
performance is measured and reported, as well as providing scheduled updates.
Nevertheless, highlights did include the City's focus on the top five most asked questions,
which is a good starting point, and its effective communication and information sharing for
services, such as snow clearing and grass cutting.
So in terms of the broad strokes, I think the biggest message is that the level of productivity,
despite COVID and the unanticipated disruption that it caused. The fact that it created absences
due to illness, it caused temporary closures, it led to some staff layoffs, it led to redeployment
of staff to other jobs, and it also led to the surfacing of some new priorities that had not
existed prior to COVID. The fact that the city, despite those disruptions, was able to complete
17 of the projects I think is really remarkable and really worthy of celebration.
So we would highly commend the city's progress in that respect.
And the other thing I would add as a note is that the two projects that did not meet our expectations
were clearly both projects that were significantly impacted by COVID,
either because it reduced the scope of the project or it led to redeployment of a small team of staff members
that held responsibility for the project.
So I think that the city staff should take great pride in what they've accomplished through that four-year time period.
In the course of our following the public engagement processes that the city has created,
as well as our review of completed projects,
there are often areas that are identified that would benefit from further attention.

So in terms of our conclusions, there are three key points we'd like to stress.
The first, going back to acknowledging and celebrating the accomplishments over the past four years,
we really applaud the 17 completed projects and the fact that 15 of the 17 have exceeded or met expectations is outstanding.
The second point relates to the strategic plan currently under development.
Given the pace of change and unpredictable elements encountered today,
it would be really beneficial to build a degree of adaptability into this and future strategic plans.
As was so well captured at an early resident panel meeting,
it's important to set a clear course of priorities and outcomes expected,
but also build in the capacity to swerve in our lane,
which was a great phrase someone came up with in that process,
as needed in order to achieve the most meaningful and impactful results for the city
using the resources available.
And the third message relates to stressing how important it is for the city
to focus on three kinds of information.
The first is data.
There would be a real benefit to tracking more data in specified areas,
which can then be used to both guide decision-making and inform evaluation of initiatives undertaken.
The second is setting and sharing meaningful outcomes at the outside of projects,
not just timelines and budgets, but meaningful outcomes addressing the intended citizen or city impact of an initiative.
And the third is providing more contextual information and doing it simply and succinctly.
Many issues that face Kitchener today are complex and their resolution involves
participation by multiple levels of government. Citizens need clear
information outlining who's responsible for what in order to truly understand
where the city can take effective action and where responsibility lies with other
levels of government. When given the necessary background information,
citizens are better equipped to focus their input on areas in which the city
can actively contribute to solving the given problem. The other aspect of
contextual information that's of key importance is the city's active
promotion of public awareness regarding the full spectrum of city actions and
decisions undertaken in a specific domain so that individual projects are
seen within that broader context. Media coverage often tends to focus in on a

attracted attention but not necessarily about the full spectrum of development
projects approved and we feel there's a real benefit to helping citizens see
individual development projects in the context of the full spectrum of
developments that are underway. And that ends our report for this evening. We're
